title: Beginner's Guide to Making Money Online: The Truth Nobody Tells You
excerpt: An honest beginner guide to building useful digital skills, avoiding online-money traps and earning without chasing shortcuts.
author: Ibrahim Sodiq

content.heading: The uncomfortable opening
content.body: A phone, internet and free time can help you start learning, but they do not automatically turn into serious money. I spent time chasing gambling, betting, trading, make-money-online schemes and shortcuts because I wanted money quickly. The hard lesson was that the boring work people avoid — coding, writing, design and real practice — is usually where the long-term value is.

content.heading: 1. There is no holy grail online
content.body: Legitimate online work asks for skill, time, knowledge, creativity, problem-solving or consistent effort. Ask who is paying, what work is being done, why the payment makes sense, whether the model is transparent, and whether claims can be checked. “Make ₦500,000 in seven days with no skills” should make you suspicious, not excited. If you must pay before you can supposedly earn, treat that as a major warning sign.

content.heading: 2. Stop chasing quick money — build a digital skill
content.body: Coding, writing and graphic design are strong examples, not the only options. Video editing, digital marketing, data analysis, UI/UX, virtual assistance, cybersecurity and specialised AI-related work can also be useful. Earning potential tends to grow when your ability, experience, reputation and usefulness grow.

content.heading: 3. Test skills instead of waiting for the perfect one
content.body: Try coding, writing, design or another skill that interests you. Give each one focused time, then ask: does it keep my attention, do I want to return to it, can I practise it consistently, and am I willing to become good at it? ChatGPT can help you explore options based on your interests, but it cannot magically choose a career for you.

content.heading: 4. You can start with a phone
content.body: I started learning coding on a phone. A phone can be enough to begin many digital skills, although coding is slower and some tools or libraries are difficult to use without a computer. Do not wait for an expensive setup before you start; improve your equipment as your ability and income grow.

content.heading: 5. Learn without drowning in tutorials
content.body: Do not collect hundreds of random tutorials. Start with fundamentals, one concept at a time, practise regularly and ask questions when stuck. You can tell an AI tutor: “I want to learn coding. I am a complete beginner. Teach me step by step and make it easy and enjoyable.” Use AI to explain ideas, not to blindly copy answers. Documentation, books and courses remain useful as you progress.

content.heading: 6. Competence first. Income follows.
content.body: Do not spend your first months asking exactly when money will arrive. That pressure can make you rush past fundamentals. Learn, practise and become comfortable with the work first. There is no honest universal timeline for income.

content.heading: 7. When to seek paid work
content.body: You do not need to be an expert before taking a small job, but you must be able to deliver it properly. Appropriate routes can include freelance and remote-work platforms, writing opportunities, AI/data-work platforms, direct clients, local businesses and professional networks. Platform rules, assessments and availability change; none guarantees work.

content.heading: 8. Make your ability visible
content.body: Build a clear LinkedIn profile, CV, portfolio, demonstration projects and professional communication. Clients need evidence. A small project that shows what you can do is more persuasive than simply saying “I know how to code.”

content.heading: 9. Writing can be an entry point
content.body: If you communicate well, writing can be a practical starting skill. Clients may give a topic, length, style, deadline and payment terms; your job is to deliver useful work. AI can assist research, brainstorming, editing and structure, but it should not replace genuine thinking or produce junk. Rejected work may become portfolio material only when client rights and confidentiality allow it.

content.heading: 10. Do not take work you cannot do
content.body: Do not pretend you can deliver a high-paying job in a language or skill you do not know. Poor work damages trust, overwhelms you and can pull you away from the skill you were actually building. Choose work you can realistically complete well.

content.heading: 11. The first money may be tiny
content.body: Your first legitimate income may be cents, a few dollars or a small freelance payment. That is not failure. The point is to separate a small temporary task from building a capability that can lead to larger opportunities.

content.heading: 12. Treat microtasks with extreme caution
content.body: Microtasks can sometimes pay small amounts, but they are not a path to wealth. Never pay money to access a supposed microtask opportunity. Check rates, withdrawal requirements, country availability, minimum payout, terms and reputation. Some tasks pay very little for the time they take.

content.heading: 13. The biggest scam warning
content.body: “Make $100 every day with no experience”, “turn ₦20,000 into ₦500,000 in one week”, “guaranteed income”, “no skills required” and “pay to unlock your account” are reasons to stop and investigate. Understand the business model before giving anyone money.

content.heading: 14. Do not quit your job too early
content.body: A safer sequence is: normal job, learn a skill, small online income, more experience, more clients, consistent income, then financial stability. Do not abandon an existing income source because you have only started learning. Multiple income sources can be safer than one risky leap.

content.heading: 15. Upgrade equipment with a reason
content.body: Start with what you have. As income grows, improve your phone, laptop, internet or tools when they genuinely make you more productive. Do not go into debt for expensive equipment before you need it.

content.heading: 16. What consistency can make possible
content.body: Two or three years of serious practice can open possibilities: remote work, freelance clients, websites, software, digital products, a business or multiple income sources. My own coding journey eventually helped me build a website, a trading bot and other projects. That is personal experience, not a promise of the same result for everyone.

content.heading: 17. A skill can become more than a job
content.body: A valuable skill can grow from freelance work to clients, reputation, business, products and multiple income streams. That path takes time, proof of work and continued learning.

content.heading: 18. The hard part is consistency
content.body: Learning gets boring, frustrating, difficult and confusing. I felt that while learning coding. Treat each error as a puzzle to solve, one step at a time. Hard work does not guarantee wealth, but quitting every difficult thing guarantees you never get the chance to improve.

content.heading: The BRYME conclusion
content.body: There is nothing wrong with wanting money. The mistake is believing money should arrive without value being created. If making money online was that easy, nobody would be doing the hard work. A phone and internet can open doors, but a valuable skill helps you walk through them. Stop chasing the shortcut. Build something valuable.

title: Website Monetization: How to Turn a Real Audience Into Revenue
excerpt: A blunt, beginner-friendly guide to building an audience, choosing legitimate monetization and protecting user trust.
author: Ibrahim Sodiq

content.heading: Build first. Monetize later.
content.body: Building a website that works, getting people to use it and monetizing it are three different jobs. A technically excellent site can make nothing if nobody visits. Before ads, know the audience, problem, reason to return and the model that fits.

content.heading: 1. Audience comes before monetization
content.body: The best investment you can make in a website is building its audience. Ad code alone does not create meaningful revenue. Visitor numbers, page views, location, engagement, time on site, returning visitors, niche and search traffic all matter. Advertising value varies; there is no honest fixed rate for every country or visitor.

content.heading: 2. Your niche matters
content.body: Research what people search for, the questions they need answered, advertiser relevance and whether a niche fits your intended monetization platform. Commercial demand can differ by topic, but no niche automatically makes money.

content.heading: 3. Getting your first audience
content.body: Start with search visibility: Google Search Console, a sitemap, useful search-friendly content, clear structure, mobile pages and internal links. Search Console helps submit, monitor and understand Google Search presence; it does not make a page rank. Early visitors can also come from WhatsApp, friends, Facebook, TikTok, relevant Reddit communities and other appropriate communities.

content.heading: 4. Give people a reason to return
content.body: One-time visitors are not the same as a real audience. Publish useful updates, build useful features, give clear reasons to return and consider subscriptions or notifications only where appropriate. The goal is for people to think, “I will come back later.”

content.heading: 5. Legitimate monetization options
content.body: There is no single best model. Google AdSense, alternative ad networks, direct advertising, affiliate links, products, services, memberships, voluntary donations and clearly labelled sponsored content can all fit different sites. Approval, earnings and availability are never guaranteed.

content.heading: Google AdSense and alternative networks
content.body: AdSense can suit websites that meet Google’s current quality and policy requirements, but approval is not guaranteed and invalid traffic or invalid clicks are prohibited. Monetag and Adsterra are alternatives some owners consider; read each provider’s current official policies, formats, traffic rules and restricted-content rules before applying. Do not use one network to bypass another network’s rules.

content.heading: Direct ads, affiliate links and your own offers
content.body: Direct sponsors can buy banner space, promoted placement or labelled sponsored content, with terms negotiated directly. Affiliate links may pay a commission for qualifying actions under a program’s terms and should be disclosed where required. A website can also sell products, services, tools, software or courses. Be clear about what is editorial and what is paid.

content.heading: 6. Do not monetize an empty website
content.body: “Welcome to my website. Here are five advertisements” is not a strategy. Establish useful content, navigation, a good experience and some returning visitors first. Establish the website, then monetize it.

content.heading: 7. Ads should not ruin the site
content.body: Ads are annoying when they are annoying. Intrusive placements can make people leave, stop returning and lose trust. Start conservatively, avoid covering important content or misleading placement, and test formats while following the provider’s current policies. Specific quantities are not universal policy.

content.heading: 8. Sustainable value beats maximum ads
content.body: More ads can create more opportunities but can also reduce reading, trust and return visits. The goal is not maximum ads. The goal is maximum sustainable value.

content.heading: 9. When to apply
content.body: Before applying, establish useful original or properly licensed content, clear purpose, functional navigation, good mobile experience, legal/policy pages, a legitimate audience and compliance with the provider you chose. Do not invent visitor or article thresholds; check official documentation.

content.heading: 10. Never buy fake traffic or click your own ads
content.body: Fake traffic wastes money, damages engagement and can cause invalid-traffic concerns, restrictions or termination. Never click your own ads, ask friends to click, create accidental-click traps, use fake download buttons or manipulate impressions. Real people who want your site are the only traffic worth building.

content.heading: 11. Copyright and honest placement matter
content.body: Do not copy articles, images, videos, logos or creative work without permission or compatible licensing. Use original, licensed or public-domain material where appropriate. Ads should look like ads, never fake navigation or site functionality.

content.heading: 12. If revenue is low, investigate
content.body: Do not panic or add dozens of ads. Look at visitor geography, page views, engagement, exits, niche, search intent, placement, formats, devices, seasonality and provider performance. Improve the website and strategy honestly; keywords alone are not a magic fix.

content.heading: 13. Diversify only when it fits
content.body: Once there is a strong audience, a site might combine ads with affiliate links, sponsors, direct advertising, products or memberships. It does not have to use every method. If users are happy and the current model works, unnecessary monetization can do more harm than good.

content.heading: 14. Do not get greedy after success
content.body: A healthy site can be ruined by extra ads, random niche changes, copyright shortcuts, fake traffic, click manipulation or chasing every revenue source. Once something works, protect it.

content.heading: The long-term model
content.body: Build → Establish → Test → Publish → Grow audience → Earn trust → Monetize → Measure → Improve. Monetization is not the finish line. Keep improving the product and giving the audience value.

content.heading: Final BRYME editorial
content.body: Build the website, establish it, test it, then give it to the world to see. Once the world loves it, monetize and get your pay. Do not build only to display ads. Build something people want, build real traffic, do not annoy visitors, and use the method that fits. Build the audience first. Monetize the value second.

title: What Upwork and Fiverr Actually Take From You in 2026
seoTitle: Upwork and Fiverr Fees in 2026: What the Platforms Actually Take
excerpt: Most fee guides online are repeating numbers the platforms have already changed. Here is what Upwork's and Fiverr's own documentation says today — and how to price so the cut does not surprise you.
author: Ibrahim Sodiq

content.heading: The number in the blog posts is not the number on your invoice
content.body:
Search for what Upwork charges and you will be told, confidently and almost everywhere, that it is a flat 10%. Search for Fiverr and you will be told the buyer pays 5.5% plus a $3 small-order fee on orders under $100. Both of those claims appear in fee guides published this year.

One of them is out of date and the other is wrong. This matters, because if you price your work off a number a content farm copied from a 2023 announcement, the shortfall comes out of your own pay.

So this guide does not cite fee calculators or comparison blogs. Every figure below comes from the platforms' own help documentation and legal terms, and the date each was checked is stated at the bottom. If a number here disagrees with something you read elsewhere, check the primary source before you trust either of us.

content.heading: Upwork: not a flat 10%, and not the same on every contract
content.body:
Upwork's own support article on the Freelancer Service Fee states that the fee "ranges from 0% to 15% per contract." There is no single platform-wide percentage any more. The fee is set per contract, based on factors Upwork describes only as supporting "a balanced and competitive environment across different types of work."

The practical consequences are more useful than the theory:

The fee is shown to you before you commit. Upwork displays the percentage when you submit a proposal or when a client sends you an offer, and you can see it later in the contract details and transaction summaries. You never have to guess which rate applies — but you do have to look, on every single contract.

Once a contract starts, the rate is locked. Upwork is explicit that once a proposal, offer or contract is sent, the fee will not change for that contract. What it will not do is stay the same across your other contracts.

The old tiered model is gone, and so is loyalty. The 20%/10%/5% sliding scale that rewarded long client relationships no longer exists. Billing a client for the hundredth time earns you no discount, and Upwork states plainly that it offers no regular discounts on the fee.

There are documented exceptions. Freelancers on Upwork Payroll pay no service fee, because they are paid through a third-party staffing firm. Any Hire contracts carry no freelancer service fee. Direct Contracts — where you bring your own client to the platform — carry a reduced fee. Enterprise client contracts are individually negotiated, though Upwork says freelancers working with Enterprise clients typically pay 10%.

content.heading: The refund rule that almost nobody mentions
content.body:
If money you were paid is refunded to the client, Upwork refunds the service fee you paid on that amount. Their worked example: $100 is returned to the client, your fee was 10%, so the $10 fee is returned to you.

This is a genuine protection and it is worth knowing before a dispute, not after. You are not charged a commission on money you did not ultimately keep. It does not, of course, refund your time.

content.heading: Fiverr: 80% to you, stated in the payment terms
content.body:
Fiverr is simpler and more expensive. Its Payment Terms, last updated January 2026, state that each completed order "credits your account with Earnings equal to 80% of the purchase amount." That is a 20% commission with no tiers, no volume discount and no loyalty reduction.

The same 80% rule is applied to hourly contracts: each completed weekly report credits you 80% of the hourly rate for the hours worked.

The one documented exception runs the other way, and it is unusual. Logo Designs sold through Fiverr's Logo Maker use a tier-based model where your share is a fixed percentage per tier, from 20% at the lowest tier up to 50% at the highest. Tiers are based on your Logo Maker sales over the previous twelve months and are recalculated on the first day of each month.

content.heading: What your Fiverr buyer pays, and why it is your problem
content.body:
The buyer-side fee is where the widely repeated numbers are wrong. Fiverr's Payment Terms state that as of September 2025 the service fee on gigs is 5.5% of the purchase amount, and that purchases under US$200 attract an additional US$3.50 small order fee.

Not $3. Not under $100. The threshold is $200 and the fee is $3.50.

That is a meaningful difference when you are setting package prices, because the small order fee is charged on a much larger share of orders than the popular guides imply. A $60 gig is a small order under Fiverr's actual rules; several fee comparison sites would tell you it is not.

Hourly contracts add one more line: a US$5 Order Initiation Fee on each new hourly contract, plus the 5.5% service fee on the hourly rate. The weekly billing cycle runs Monday 00:00 UTC to Sunday 23:59 UTC, with buyers charged automatically each Monday.

None of this comes out of your 80%. It still matters, because it is the number your buyer sees at checkout, and it shapes what they are willing to accept as your headline price.

content.heading: Getting the money out
content.body:
Fiverr publishes its withdrawal fees directly in the payment terms, charged by its payment service providers rather than by Fiverr:

PayPal costs US$0. The Fiverr Revenue Card, operated by Payoneer, costs US$1 within two days or US$3 within two hours, and is available worldwide except in India and Russia. Local Bank Transfer, also via Payoneer, costs US$3 per transfer and is available worldwide. Direct Deposit (ACH) costs US$1 per transfer and is US-only.

Two cautions that apply to anyone paid outside the United States. First, Fiverr notes that the provider you choose may apply additional fees based on your location and currency. Second, your Fiverr balance is always derived from its US dollar value, so the local-currency amount moves daily with exchange rates and includes conversion fees. You always have the option to withdraw in US dollars.

There is also a rule worth knowing before you ever need it: earnings from a disabled account can only be withdrawn after a 90-day safety period following full verification of account ownership.

Upwork's withdrawal options and their costs are documented separately from the service fee article cited here, and vary by country and method — check them against your own account rather than against any figure quoted in a guide, including this one.

content.heading: Pricing so the fee is not a surprise
content.body:
The arithmetic freelancers get wrong is subtracting the fee instead of dividing by what is left.

If you want to keep $20 an hour and the fee is 10%, you do not charge $22. You charge your target divided by 0.90, which is $22.22 — and this is exactly the example Upwork uses in its own documentation. Charging $22 leaves you $19.80.

The general rule: your rate equals your target take-home divided by (1 minus the fee rate). At Fiverr's 20%, keeping $100 means charging $125, not $120. At Upwork's maximum 15%, keeping $100 means charging $117.65.

Because Upwork's fee is now per-contract rather than fixed, this calculation has to be redone for each contract instead of once. Read the percentage on the offer screen before you accept it. Upwork provides a built-in rate calculator that estimates net pay after the fee, and it notes that rounding can shift the final figure by a cent or two in either direction.

content.heading: What this does not tell you
content.body:
Fees are the easiest part of platform economics to verify and the least important part of whether the work is worth doing.

This guide makes no claim about which platform will earn you more, how quickly you can expect a first order, or what a realistic income is. Those depend on your category, your portfolio, your competition and your timing, and anyone who quotes you a confident number for them is guessing.

What you can take from this: the commission is knowable, it is published, and it is different from what most of the internet says it is. Check it on the source, price by dividing rather than subtracting, and re-check whenever you start a new contract — because on Upwork the rate is now a per-contract variable, and on Fiverr the buyer-side thresholds have already moved once since September 2025.

sources.name: Upwork — Learn about the Freelancer Service Fee
Fiverr — Terms of Service (last updated January 2026)

title: Writing Field Notes: How I Research Sites, Write to Them, and What I Will Not Fake
seoTitle: Writing Field Notes: Research, Applications, No Guaranteed Gigs
excerpt: Writing is the online skill that has actually paid me. This is the process I use instead of buying scripts: research a website, write to them, publish what happened. A gig is not guaranteed.
author: Ibrahim Sodiq

content.heading: The only method that has paid me so far
content.body:
I have chased the usual shortcuts. Writing is the thing that has actually produced money. Not because writing is easy, and not because the internet owes anyone a gig. Because a website that needs words will sometimes pay a person who can deliver them.

That is the whole idea behind BRYME Writing Field Notes. I research real publications. I write to them when I am going to talk about them. I publish what happened — including silence. Then, on YouTube, I walk through about three of those notes and how the money path actually works. If you want the dates, the apply links and the leftover sites from that month, they live on the field-notes page.

A gig is not guaranteed. Anyone selling you a script that skips this part is selling hope.

content.heading: What this series is not
content.body:
It is not a directory of every website that has ever had a write-for-us page.

It is not a promise that publications accept writers from Nigeria, or that they pay on time, or that they still run the programme you saw in a 2023 screenshot.

It is not a course. I will not ask you to pay to unlock a list.

If a row on the field-notes page does not have a date, treat it as unfinished. If I did not email them, I will not invent how long they take to reply.

content.heading: The process, in the order I actually do it
content.body:
First I pick a niche I can write. Tech explainers, money explainers, entertainment — only if I can produce a piece I would put my name on. Applying for medical or legal content I cannot stand behind is how you get rejected and deserve it.

Second I find the real door: a contributor page, an editor address, a form. I copy the URL. I read two or three of their recent pieces so the pitch is not generic.

Third I record the date I applied, what I sent, and what they asked for. That log is the product. Memory is how people start lying to themselves.

Fourth I wait. I do not send five follow-ups in a week. If nothing comes back, the note says “no reply as of this date.” That is a complete note.

Fifth, if they reply, I write down the brief, the pay if they named it, and the payment method if they named it. I do not upgrade “we will be in touch” into “I landed the gig.”

content.heading: Country is not a bonus filter. It is the point.
content.body:
Most public lists of “sites that pay writers” are written for people with a US or UK payment setup. From Lagos, the questions that actually matter are narrower.

Do they accept work from Nigeria, or do they quietly drop those emails?
Do they pay through a method that arrives here, or only through a method that does not?
Did they say any of this in writing, or am I guessing from a comment section?

I start these notes from Nigeria because that is where I write from. Other countries can be added later, the same way: one writer, dated applications, no copied reply times. If I do not know whether a site takes your country, the page will say unknown. Unknown is honest. “They hire worldwide” without evidence is not.

content.heading: How money actually moves — when it moves
content.body:
A typical paid path looks like this: you apply, they ask for a sample or a pitch, they give a brief, you write, they edit, they publish, they pay through the method they already use.

Any of those steps can stop. A killed draft is not a payment. A published piece with “exposure” and no invoice is unpaid work, and I will label it unpaid.

I will not publish a rate I did not see on their site or in their email. I will not publish a payout timeline I did not live. If their page is silent on money, the field-notes card will say unknown.

Earnings vary. The first legitimate writing money can be small. That is not a reason to buy a script. It is a reason to treat writing as a skill you practise, not a jackpot.

content.heading: What I log for every site
content.body:
Name and niche.
The apply URL and the method — email, form, or pitch.
Whether they say they pay, do not pay, or do not say.
Payment methods they have named, if any.
The country I wrote from.
Whether I contacted them, and on which date.
Whether they replied, and on which date.
Whether I landed a gig, and whether I was paid.
What they want, who should skip them, and what is still unknown.
The date I last checked the page.

If a field would require a guess, I leave it empty and list it under unknowns.

content.heading: The YouTube half
content.body:
Each video covers about three sites I have already logged. The video should still be useful if you never open BRYME: what they publish, how I applied, what they said about money, and what happened in my inbox.

The website is for the parts that are awkward on camera — the exact links, the dates, the sites I researched but did not feature, and the updates when a programme closes.

I will not make “go to my website for the real list” videos that withhold the answer. If the answer is “they did not reply,” you will hear that in the video.

content.heading: Why this is better than buying a script
content.body:
A bought script is usually someone else’s voice, written for a different country, sold to people who do not want to send the email.

This method is slower. You will be ignored. You will write samples that nobody uses. You will also have a dated sentence you can stand behind: I wrote to them on this day, and this is what happened.

That sentence is reusable. A script is not. If writing never pays you, you still practised. If a script never pays you, you are only out of money.

content.heading: Where the live list lives
content.body:
The dated cards are on the Writing Field Notes page. This article is the rulebook. When a YouTube video goes up, the same page will carry the link.

I update a row when I re-check it. I do not delete a closed programme just to look current — a dated “closed” helps the next person more than a disappearing URL.

If you want the honest version of online writing, start there. If you want a guarantee, I do not have one.
